Correct though technically it represented the two gauges on a radio receiver: one for signal strength and the other for signal clarity. Each gauge had a range between 1 and 5. So when a signal was loud and clear the receiving station would say "I have you 5 by 5". That later turned into just a generic term when you could hear someone over the radio clearly such as a WW II pilot receiving a message message over his radio which did not have the two gauges but could hear the message clearly would respond "I have you 5 by 5" or "I have you loud and clear".

There are a number of variations. In Vietnam (I was a Marine platoon commander) my radio operator, Lance Corporal James Jones or JJ for short, would often answer an incoming radio message would answer "Echo, this is Echo 2, roger, I have you 5." Translation: Echo Company radio operator, this is Echo Company 2nd Platoon radio operator, roger, I have you loud and clear."

It was important because much of the time in Vietnam (at least where I was) radio coms were poor to none, depending on whether we were in a valley, jungle, monsoon season, or just too far away. Most of the time we operated separately from the company and we would be perhaps 10 miles apart. There was also the noise during a battle that made understanding an incoming radio transmission difficult. I remember JJ screaming into the radio during firefights, not because he was excited, but because he was trying to talk over the deafening noise: M-16's, M-60 MG's, AK-47's, grenades, mortars, artillery, bombs, and people screaming orders and wounded crying for help. Pure chaos and carnage.

All the movies I've seen about Vietnam with two exceptions were worthless. We Were Soldiers with Mel Gibson was far more intense than what I experienced but a friend of mine who was in that battle told me it was 90 percent accurate except at the end. For me it may seem odd, but I thought the Vietnam battle scene in Forest Gump was pretty damn close to what I experienced.

Movies such as Platoon, Deer Hunter, and Apocalypse Now had nothing to do with anything I saw in Vietnam.

After I retired from the Marine Corps, I provided some technical support (long story) to both Special Forces and National Missions forces worldwide for about 7 years. One of my friends was a retired Delta Force company commander who told me that the movie Blackhawk Down was about 80 percent accurate.

I digress.

Hard to believe that I arrived in Vietnam 50 years ago next week. It wasn't the Merriest Christmas or Happiest New Year I have ever had, but the experience changed me forever--mostly for the better and some not so much.

Also hard to believe I survived it all. I was physically exhausting, but sometimes the hardest part was the mental stress. Everyday in the back of your mind you wondered if you'd see the sunset and every night you wondered if you'd see the sunrise. Mines and booby-traps were everywhere. Too many good Marines in my platoon didn't those sunsets or sunrises. I have always wonder "why them and not me?" I still think about that.

It wasn't all serious. I have a lot of humorous stories. Well, they were humorous to me, but if you've never been in combat, you might consider it "dark humor."

My apologies for the rambling. I'm 72 now and I don't hear 5 by 5 anymore. Too many ear busting noises a very long time ago.
